candidateAnswers.argumentAgainst: It assumes apparent turn is a single angle, which may be false: a figure can read as turned because of its face and shoulders while its body is nearly square.
candidateAnswers.argumentFor: It is computable, it extends to seats nobody has drawn yet, and it turns the hand-written permission lists into something derived.
candidateAnswers.label: Angle agreement within a tolerance
candidateAnswers.position: A seat records the angle it is drawn at, a figure records the angle it is drawn at, and a figure reads as seated when the two are within some stated number of degrees.

candidateAnswers.argumentAgainst: If it is wrong we would be filling angled seats with square figures and only find out when somebody looks at a finished room.
candidateAnswers.argumentFor: It would explain why square figures have looked acceptable in angled chairs so far, and we already measure the contact point.
candidateAnswers.label: Contact and occlusion carry it, not angle
candidateAnswers.position: What sells a seated figure is that its hips meet the seat surface and its near leg reads in front of the chair's near edge. Turn agreement is secondary and a wide mismatch passes unnoticed.

notes: This is a question about what a viewer perceives, not about our data. We can measure anything about our own plates that an answer asks us to measure.
A room is first person, so the seated figure is usually another person in the room with the player rather than the player themselves.
question: When a room's seat is drawn at an angle to the camera and a person is composed onto it from a separate flat plate, what has to agree between the two for the result to read as that person sitting in that chair rather than near it — how closely must the figure's own turn match the seat's drawn angle, how much mismatch is tolerable before a viewer notices, and what should a seat and a figure each record so a room can decide this by rule instead of somebody deciding by eye?

sourcesChecked.source: art/manifest/pose_families.json, which declares each pose family's posture and facing
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: It records which way a figure faces, and a seat records which facings it permits, but permission is a yes or no list written by hand. Nothing says how far apart the two may be, so the list is an assertion rather than a derivation.

sourcesChecked.source: The turn measurement in scripts/art-asset-factory/seated-contact.ts, and the twelve seated plates measured through it
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: It gives each figure a signed turn offset, so we can compare figures to each other. It says nothing about what a viewer accepts, because there is no measurement of a chair's drawn angle to compare it against and no evidence about tolerance.

The chair is drawn turned towards the room and permits one facing. Whether a figure carrying that facing actually looks seated in it was left as a judgement to be made by eye, which is the gap this question is about.

title: What makes a drawn sitting figure read as sitting in this particular chair
usableAnswer: A stated rule with a number in it — for example, that a figure reads as seated when its turn is within some stated angle of the seat's drawn angle, or that turn agreement matters less than a named cue such as where the near knee falls — together with which properties a seat and a figure each have to carry for a room to apply that rule without a person looking.
whyItMatters: Every seated placement in the project is currently settled by looking at it. We can measure a figure's turn and the point where it meets a seat, and we do, but nothing tells us whether a figure turned one way belongs in a seat drawn another way, so the last step before a person appears in a chair is a judgement nobody can check or repeat. That makes seated coverage un-plannable: we cannot say which seats our existing people can fill, or what to ask for when they cannot.
